title: Pointer arithmetic: moving a pointer through memory

visuals.title: p + 1 moves one whole int (made-up addresses)

steps.note: Five ints, each 4 bytes after the one before: 0x1000, 0x1004, 0x1008, 0x100C, 0x1010.
arr means the address of its first element. p stores 0x1000 and points to arr[0].
p + 2 is the address 0x1000 + 2 x 4 = 0x1008, which is arr[2]. The pointer p itself does not move. *(p + 2) is 30, the same as arr[2].
p++ moves p to the next int: 0x1004, not 0x1001. Now p points to arr[1].
p moves two ints (8 bytes) ahead to 0x100C and points to arr[3], value 40.

goal: After this you can say where p + 1, p++ and p - q end up, use *(p + i) instead of arr[i], compare pointers, and name the arithmetic that is NOT allowed.
warmup: Imagine a row of seats in a cinema, each seat the same width. If you are on seat 5 and you move 3 seats to the right, you do not measure in centimetres. You just count seats: you are now on seat 8. A pointer does the same. p + 3 means move three ELEMENTS forward, and the computer works out the bytes for you: 3 ints = 12 bytes.
definition: Pointer arithmetic means adding or subtracting whole numbers to a pointer. Adding 1 does not add 1 byte. It moves the pointer to the next element of its own type, which means it adds sizeof(type) bytes. For an int * on our computers, p + 1 is 4 bytes ahead. The array name is the address of the first element, so for int *p = arr; the expression *(p + i) is the same as arr[i].
howItWorks: Run the memory picture. The array elements are 4 bytes apart, so the addresses go 0x1000, 0x1004, 0x1008 and so on. Here is the rule: p + n has the address p + n x sizeof(type). If p is an int * at 1000, then p + 1 is 1004, p + 3 is 1012, p++ makes p itself become 1004, and p-- moves it back. Notice the difference between p + 1 (gives a new address, p stays) and p++ (changes p). Two pointers into the same array can be subtracted: q - p gives the number of elements between them (not bytes). They can also be compared with == != < > <= >=. What is NOT allowed: adding two pointers, multiplying or dividing a pointer, and subtracting pointers of different types or different arrays. Last, a trap: *p++ means take the value, then move the pointer (the ++ belongs to p). (*p)++ means increase the value p points to, and p stays. And stay inside the array: moving a pointer beyond the last element and using * there reads memory that is not yours.
syntax:
int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int *p = arr;          // p points to arr[0]

*(p + 2)    // 30, same as arr[2]; p does not move
p++;        // p now points to arr[1]
p--;        // back to arr[0]
p += 2;     // p now points to arr[2]

int *q = &arr[4];
cout << q - p;     // number of ELEMENTS between them
cout << (p < q);   // comparison: 1 (true)

*p++       // use the value, then move p
(*p)++     // increase the value, p stays

sample.title: Walking through an array with a pointer

explanation.text: arr is the address of the first element, so p points to arr[0].
p + i is the address of element i. The * reads the value there. It is the same as arr[i].
Moves p to the next int (4 bytes ahead).
Moves p two elements forward, to arr[3].

steps.note: Five ints side by side in memory, 4 bytes each.
An array name stands for the address of its first element. So p points to arr[0].
The loop starts with i = 0.
p + 0 is p itself, so *(p + 0) is arr[0] = 10. p does not move.
p + 1 is the address 1 elements after p. *(p + 1) reads arr[1] = 20. p itself does NOT move.
p + 2 is the address 2 elements after p. *(p + 2) reads arr[2] = 30. p itself does NOT move.
p + 3 is the address 3 elements after p. *(p + 3) reads arr[3] = 40. p itself does NOT move.
p + 4 is the address 4 elements after p. *(p + 4) reads arr[4] = 50. p itself does NOT move.
p++ moves p to the NEXT int: 4 bytes ahead, not 1. Now p points to arr[1].
*p is arr[1] = 20.
p += 2 moves p two ints (8 bytes) ahead. Now p points to arr[3].
*p is arr[3] = 40.

sample.title: Difference and comparison of pointers
sample.expectedOutput:
Elements between: 5
Bytes between: 20
first < last? 1
*mid = 20
mid - first = 3

explanation.text: first points to the first element.
last points to the last element, 5 elements later.
Subtracting two pointers into the same array gives the number of ELEMENTS between them: 5.
As plain numbers the addresses are 5 x 4 = 20 bytes apart. The pointer difference already divided by 4 for us.
Pointers into the same array can be compared. first comes earlier, so this is true (1).
first + 3 is the address of arr[3].
Moving first forward by 5 elements lands exactly on last: true.

sample.title: The *p++ versus (*p)++ trap

explanation.text: Use the value, then move the pointer.
The brackets make ++ act on the value, not on the pointer.
Pointer minus array start gives the element index: 3.

steps.note: An array of 4 ints.
p points to a[0].
*p++ reads the value p points to (3) and THEN moves p to the next element. The ++ belongs to the pointer.
p now points to a[1], so *p is 6.
(*p)++ increases the VALUE p points to. a[1] goes from 6 to 7. p does not move.
a[1] is 7 and *p is the same box, 7.
p moves two elements forward from a[1] to a[3].
*p is a[3] = 12. p - a counts the elements between a[0] and a[3]: 3.

No compiler error. The program reads memory beyond the array, which gives a garbage value or can crash. Valid elements are *(p + 0) to *(p + 4).

mistakes.wrong: int x = *p++;   // student wants x = value and then value + 1
mistakes.right:
int x = *p;
(*p)++;   // increase the value, not the pointer
mistakes.error: No compiler error. *p++ moves the POINTER, so p now points to the next element and the value is not increased.

examTips: Learn the rule: p + n moves n x sizeof(type) bytes. For int * one step is 4 bytes, so p + 3 from 1000 is 1012.
*(p + i) is identical to arr[i]. Write both when an exam asks you to rewrite array code with pointers.
Pointer minus pointer gives ELEMENTS, not bytes. If the question wants bytes, multiply by the size of the type.
Allowed: pointer + integer, pointer - integer, ++, --, pointer - pointer, comparisons. NOT allowed: pointer + pointer, pointer * integer, pointer / integer.
Trace *p++ and (*p)++ carefully: first one moves p, second one changes the value. Draw an arrow and move it.
romanSummary: Pointer mein 1 jama karne se 1 byte nahi, balke poora ek element aage jata hai. int * ke liye yeh 4 bytes hain.
p + i array ke i-th element ka address deta hai, aur *(p + i) bilkul arr[i] jaisa hai.
p++ pointer ko agle element par le jata hai aur p-- pichle par.
Ek hi array ke do pointers ka farq (q - p) elements ki ginti deta hai. Do pointers jama ya multiply nahi kar sakte.
*p++ pehle value use karta hai phir pointer aage karta hai, jab ke (*p)++ value ko barhata hai aur pointer wahin rehta hai.

quiz.prompt: For an int pointer p, what does p + 1 do?
options: Gives the address of the next int
quiz.answer: Gives the address of the next int
quiz.hint: It moves by the size of the type.
quiz.explanation: p + 1 adds sizeof(int) bytes, moving to the next element.

quiz.prompt: Which expression is the same as arr[i] when int *p = arr;?
quiz.explanation: *(p + i) reads the value at the address p + i, exactly arr[i].

quiz.prompt: Which operation on two pointers is NOT allowed?
quiz.hint: It makes no sense to add two addresses.
quiz.explanation: Pointer + pointer is not allowed. Subtraction and comparison are.

quiz.prompt: int a[3] = {5, 6, 7}; int *p = a; What does *p++ evaluate to?
quiz.hint: The value is read before p moves.
quiz.explanation: *p++ uses the value at p (5) and then moves p to the next element.

options: Increases the value p points to; p stays
Moves p to the next element
quiz.answer: Increases the value p points to; p stays
quiz.explanation: The brackets make ++ act on the value, not the pointer.
